entities.summary:
James of Viterbo, born Giacomo Capocci, was an Italian Roman Catholic Augustinian friar and Scholastic theologian who later became Archbishop of Naples.

Born in unknown year, James of Viterbo was educated in Bologna and later became a prominent figure in the Scholastic movement. He was ordained as a priest in 1279 and served as a canon in the cathedral of Brescia before being appointed as Archbishop of Naples in 1305.

As Archbishop, James of Viterbo played a key role in the Catholic Church's relations with the Kingdom of Sicily and the Holy Roman Empire. He also continued his theological work, producing several influential treatises on Scholastic theology.

James of Viterbo died in 1308, leaving behind a legacy as a prominent figure in the Catholic Church and a significant contributor to the development of Scholastic theology.

In a notable twist, James of Viterbo's appointment as Archbishop of Naples was influenced by the Catholic Church's efforts to assert its authority in the region following the decline of the Kingdom of Sicily.

The years of James of Viterbo's tenure as Archbishop saw significant theological debates and ecclesiastical reforms within the Catholic Church.

James of Viterbo's work on Scholastic theology had a lasting impact on the development of Catholic doctrine, influencing prominent theologians such as Duns Scotus and William of Ockham.

Despite his influence, James of Viterbo's life remains somewhat of a mystery, with many details of his personal life and theological contributions still subject to scholarly debate and interpretation.
